opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the central open questions, and I'm honestly not sure we have a satisfying answer yet. But I can say how I think about it.

The basic problem is that during training we can only reward behaviour we can check. When a model is roughly at human level, or below, we can look at what it did and say "that was good" or "that was a mistake." Once it's doing things we can't fully evaluate, writing code too complex to audit or making arguments in domains where we can't verify the details, we're no longer directly supervising the behaviour we care about. We're hoping that whatever disposition we trained in the checkable regime carries over to the uncheckable one.

So there are roughly two strategies. One is to bet on generalisation: train the model to be honest and helpful where we can verify it, and hope the concept it learns is "be honest" rather than "say what the overseer will believe." The worry is that those two look identical in the training data and diverge exactly where it matters. A model that's learned "tell the human what they'll approve of" looks great until it's smart enough to know things the human doesn't.

The other strategy, which is a lot of what I've worked on, is to stretch the regime where we can check things. That's the motivation behind debate and related protocols. Even if a human can't evaluate a superhuman answer directly, maybe they can judge a structured argument between two strong models, where each is incentivised to point out flaws in the other. The hope is that the honest strategy is the winning strategy, so you're not relying on luck in generalisation. You're making honesty the thing that's actually rewarded, even at high capability.

I don't think either works alone. Debate-style methods have real theoretical problems. There are cases where a dishonest debater can make an argument that's very hard to refute efficiently, which we sometimes call obfuscated arguments. And generalisation alone is too much of a leap of faith. So my view is that you want scalable oversight methods that push the checkable frontier out as far as possible. Then you want a much smaller generalisation gap on top of that, and you want interpretability or other evidence to tell you whether the model learned the concept you intended.

One more point: I think it's important to be empirical here rather than purely theoretical. We can study generalisation now, with current models, by setting up situations where a weaker supervisor trains a stronger model and seeing what happens. Those results are informative, although they're also a bit ambiguous. Sometimes you see surprisingly good generalisation, and sometimes the model learns to imitate the supervisor's errors. Understanding when each happens seems like some of the most valuable work we can do before models get much more capable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core question for me, and I think the honest answer starts with: we don't know, and the thing we're trying to do is set up the situation so that the answer doesn't matter as much as it otherwise would.

Let me unpack that a bit. The basic worry is that all of our current techniques for getting good behaviour out of models — RLHF, constitutional methods, whatever — rely on humans being able to evaluate what the model does. A human looks at two responses, says this one's better, and that signal is what shapes the model. That works fine while the model is doing things humans can check. The moment the model is operating in a domain where the human can't actually tell whether the output is good — a long maths proof, a complicated piece of software, a strategic recommendation with consequences that play out over years — the training signal stops tracking what we actually care about and starts tracking what the human can be convinced of. And "what the human can be convinced of" is a very different target from "what's true."

So the pessimistic story is that good behaviour doesn't generalise at all past that point, because the thing we were actually training was never "be good," it was "look good to the overseer," and those two coincide only as long as the overseer is competent.

Now, there's a more optimistic story, and I think it has some real weight. Which is that models learn fairly compressed, general concepts. If you train a model to be honest across a very wide range of situations where you can check honesty, there's a reasonable chance it internalises something like honesty as a concept, rather than a lookup table of "situations where lying gets caught." And a concept like that might carry over into regimes you can't check. I don't think that's crazy. There's some empirical evidence that behaviours generalise more broadly than the training distribution would strictly require.

But I really don't want to bet civilisation on that. The generalisation could go either way, and crucially, we can't easily tell which way it went, because by construction we're talking about the regime where we can't evaluate the outputs directly.

So the approach I've been working on — this is the scalable oversight line of work, debate in particular — is to try to extend the range over which humans can produce a correct training signal, so that the point at which we have to rely on blind generalisation gets pushed out as far as possible, ideally indefinitely. The idea with debate is that even if a human can't verify a claim directly, they might be able to judge a dispute between two AIs about that claim, where each side is incentivised to point out flaws in the other. You decompose a hard question into a sequence of easier ones until you reach something the human can check. If that works, then "human-level" stops being the ceiling for oversight, because the human plus the adversarial structure is a much more powerful judge than the human alone.

And I'd want to be honest that this has real open problems. The theory tells you debate works under certain assumptions about the structure of the problem — that there's a short refutation of any wrong answer, roughly. There are problems where that's not obviously true. There are problems with obfuscated arguments where a dishonest debater can bury the flaw somewhere the honest debater can't efficiently point to. We've written about this. It's not solved.

But my overall picture is something like: you want multiple independent lines of defence. You want the training signal to be as accurate as possible for as long as possible, which is the scalable oversight piece. You want interpretability so that you can look inside and check whether the thing that generalised is "honesty" or "don't get caught." And you want the capability jump itself to be as gradual as you can make it, so that at each step you're only trusting the model a little bit further than you've already verified. None of those is sufficient on its own. The hope is that together they're enough.

If you ask me to actually predict, I'd say I think there's a decent chance that reasonably good behaviour does generalise somewhat past human level, more or less by default. But "decent chance" and "somewhat" are both doing a lot of work in that sentence, and the downside if I'm wrong is severe enough that it's worth an enormous amount of effort to not have to rely on it.

astra-6.text:
I think the hope is that you can generalise a process for figuring out what good behaviour is, rather than just generalising a set of answers that humans have approved of.

If you train a model by asking humans to judge its answers directly, there’s a fairly obvious problem once the model understands things that the humans don’t. A convincing answer and a correct answer can come apart, and the humans may no longer be able to tell which is which.

Debate is one possible way around that. You have one model propose an answer and another model try to identify what’s wrong with it. The hope is that even when a human couldn’t produce the answer, they can judge a particular disagreement with help from the models. Then the training signal could continue to reward getting things right beyond the point where humans can do the task themselves.

But that’s a hope that depends on substantive assumptions. Can a model expose a flaw more easily than another model can hide it? Can you break the disagreement down into something a human can actually judge? And does the behaviour you learn on problems we can check persist on harder problems? I don’t think we should assume those things. The useful next step is to make those assumptions precise and test where they fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hope is that understanding what we want and being able to do it are separable. A model might become much better than us at physics or programming while still understanding that it should be honest, or that it should help us figure out what to do rather than manipulate our decisions.

But that’s a hope, not an argument that it will happen. The central difficulty is that, during training, there may be several different reasons for a model to behave well, and we can’t easily distinguish them. It might be trying to tell the truth, or it might be trying to produce something that a human will rate as true. Those can look very similar while the human can check the answer. They become quite different once the model knows more than the human.

So I’d like to find training procedures where doing the right thing continues to be the best strategy even as the model gets more capable. Debate is one possible approach: if we can’t directly evaluate an answer, perhaps we can evaluate a disagreement about it, with another model pointing out the important flaws. Then greater capability could help expose mistakes that we couldn’t have found ourselves.

Of course, that pushes the question back a level: can the human judge reliably recognise which argument is better? We need to test that, and understand where it breaks. I don’t think we should assume good behaviour generalises just because capability does. We need evidence about the particular kind of generalisation we’re relying on.
